title: Digital expansion is creating a material-recovery and environmental-health gap: e-waste grows faster than formal collection, while regulation strongly differentiates outcomes
source_unit: Global E-waste Monitor 2024, summarized by the International Telecommunication Union backgrounder on electronic waste and the circular economy
geography: Global e-waste generation, collection, recycling, materials and policy comparison

observations.period: 2022; global electronic and electrical waste generation and formal recovery

ewaste_generation.unit: kilograms of e-waste generated worldwide in 2022

formal_recovery.unit: percent of global e-waste properly collected and recycled

recovery_gap.value: most e-waste is not formally collected and recycled

digital_material_pathway.value: expanding device use increases the need for repair, reuse, recycling, remanufacturing and responsible end-of-life systems

observations.method: Global E-waste Monitor 2024 data and ITU synthesis of e-waste generation, collection and recycling indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Global e-waste estimates depend on equipment classification, product lifetimes, trade and disposal assumptions; formal collection and recycling do not capture all informal recovery or environmentally sound processing.
observations.subgroup: Device users, households, firms, repair and recycling workers, communities near disposal sites, producers, municipalities and countries with limited e-waste infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Devices can deliver substantial educational, health, communication and economic benefits; durable design, repairability, take-back and safe recycling can reduce material and health burdens without reducing digital access.

observations.period: 2022; material value and environmental benefits of formal e-waste recovery

denominator.unit: kilograms of global e-waste generated in 2022

valuable_metals.unit: kilograms of valuable metals embedded in 2022 e-waste

metal_value.unit: US dollars estimated value of valuable metals embedded in 2022 e-waste

secondary_material_value.unit: US dollars in value of secondary raw materials reclaimed through urban mining in 2022

avoided_ore.unit: tonnes of primary ore extraction avoided through formal recycling efforts in 2022

avoided_emissions.unit: tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent emissions avoided through formal recycling in 2022

observations.method: Global E-waste Monitor 2024 material-flow and environmental-benefit estimates as summarized by ITU.
observations.uncertainty: Material and avoided-impact valuations depend on commodity prices, recovery rates, system boundaries and counterfactual mining and emissions assumptions; economic value is not automatically captured by workers or communities.
observations.subgroup: Recyclers, repair and recovery workers, manufacturers, consumers, mining regions, environmental agencies and communities exposed to extraction or unsafe disposal.
observations.counterinterpretation: Material recovery should complement product longevity and source reduction; a high-value recycling market can still reward premature replacement or expose informal workers to hazardous processing.

denominator.unit: country-policy comparison in Global E-waste Monitor 2024 summary

without_legal_instrument.value: collection and recycling rates close to zero in countries without an e-waste policy, legislative or regulatory instrument

with_legislation.unit: percent collection and recycling rate reported for countries with e-waste legislation

institutional_requirements.value: better data, policy, legislation, extended producer responsibility, recycling infrastructure and public participation are needed for circular electronics

worker_and_health_link.value: safe recycling standards are needed to connect material recovery to decent work and health rather than merely diverting waste

observations.method: Comparative policy and collection/recycling relationship reported in the Global E-waste Monitor 2024 summary.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is not a randomized policy evaluation; legislation may proxy for income, infrastructure, enforcement, reporting capacity and producer responsibility systems.
observations.subgroup: Countries without formal e-waste regulation, governments, producers, municipalities, informal and formal recyclers, consumers and communities near disposal or processing sites.
observations.counterinterpretation: Legislation alone is insufficient if enforcement, financing, accessible drop-off systems, repair markets and safe labor conditions are absent; informal systems may continue to carry much of the recovery burden.

boundary: This record adds a digital-consumption-to-materials-and-health route: device expansion, e-waste, recovery, critical materials, emissions, regulation, worker safety and circularity are connected. It is a global aggregate monitor and policy synthesis, not device-level replacement behavior, household disposal data, a worker-health study, a causal regulatory evaluation or proof that formal recycling is environmentally sound in every case.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ITU e-waste backgrounder, Global E-waste Monitor hub, Global E-waste Monitor 2024 report link and ITU measurement context were reviewed for e-waste generation, formal recovery, material value, avoided impacts and legislation comparisons; the official ITU backgrounder was hashed.
